MEMO

TO: Members of the City Council, City of Greenfield
FROM: Office of Management and Budget — Management Analysis Unit
DATE: October 19, 2026
RE: Departmental Restructuring Decision — Analysis of Proposal A (Consolidation) and Proposal B (Targeted Fix), with Recommended Hybrid Approach

1. Purpose and Recommendation Summary

This memorandum presents the cost-benefit analysis supporting the Council's upcoming vote on the departmental restructuring. Two proposals were modeled against the FY2024 baseline:

- Proposal A ("Consolidate") merges Health Services and Parks & Recreation into a Community Wellness department, and Sanitation and Transportation into a Public Works department; Fire remains standalone.
- Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") retains all five departments and adds a centralized hiring unit for high-vacancy divisions, cross-training pools, and shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding a 10% overtime-to-regular-hours threshold.

Recommended action: Adopt Proposal B as the primary operating framework, supplemented by (i) a voluntary Sanitation–Transportation "Shared Fleet & Routing Compact" that captures the interdepartmental coordination benefit Proposal A sought through full merger, without the governance risk, and (ii) an automation triage program targeting the eight manual, below-threshold processes. Head-to-head, Proposal B produces marginally higher annual savings ($531,991 vs $517,954), nearly seven times the service-delivery improvement (SLA lift +6.9 vs +2.9 points; below-threshold processes reduced from 8 to 3 vs 8 to 6), a lower implementation risk rating (2 vs 3 on a 5-point scale), and a materially larger workforce stabilization effect (27 FTE reallocated vs 4). A weighted net score (savings 25%, SLA improvement 30%, complexity 20%, risk 25%) yields 2.89 for B versus 1.81 for A.

2. Situation Overview: Staffing Health and Service Outcomes

2.1 Workforce position. Greenfield's five operating departments are authorized for 596 positions; 542 are filled, leaving 54 vacancies (9.1%). Payroll is $28.39M; overtime adds $4.35M (9.6% of 1,141,177 regular hours), for total personnel cost of $32.74M.

Table 1 — FY2024 department scorecard (red flags: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%)

[table]

Three findings stand out:

1. Vacancy is concentrated, not evenly distributed. All eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger are in Transportation (14.8–15.8% by division) and Health Services (13.6–18.2%); together these divisions hold 230 authorized positions and 36 vacancies (15.7%). Transportation's 14.9% departmental vacancy rate and Health's 16.7% are the direct drivers of the citywide 9.1%.
2. Overtime is a Fire Department problem first. Fire accounts for 47.9% of citywide OT spend ($2.09M of $4.35M) at the highest rate in the workforce ($48.00/hr) and exceeded the 10% OT-to-regular-hours threshold in all 12 months of FY2024. Sanitation sits on the watchlist (9.8% annual, but above 10% in four winter months — 52.9% of its annual OT falls in November–March, $342,302), while Parks is summer-concentrated (44.6% of its OT in May–August, $202,540). The two seasonal patterns are complementary — an argument for cross-training rather than merger.
3. Service outcomes track staffing health. Transportation has the worst 311 performance (13.6-day average resolution; 45.2-day Street Resurfacing cycle against a 30-day target; 48.3% on-time) and the lowest satisfaction (3.36/5.0). Health Services' high-priority requests average 13.9 days — the worst in the city. Citywide, of 500 FY2024 311 requests, 437 closed and 63 remain open; the weighted average resolution is 10.8 days; 44 requests (10.1%) exceeded 30 days; weighted satisfaction is 3.63/5.0.

2.4 The cross-cutting bottleneck is automation, not structure. Of 25 mapped processes, the 8 below the 65% on-time threshold are all Manual. Manual processes average 63.6% on-time, 5.9% error, and 16.1-day cycles; Semi-Automated average 80.8% / 3.7% / 4.1 days; Automated 94.8% / 1.4% / 1.1 days. Neither proposal as written addresses this gap (see Recommendation, §7).

3. NYC Benchmark Context

3.1 Staffing trends (NYS Comptroller, Report 2-2025). New York City's post-pandemic experience frames Greenfield's choices. Citywide vacancy peaked at 8.4% (Dec 2022) and stood at 5.1% in January 2024 — still 2.5x the pre-pandemic 2.0%. Greenfield's 9.1% exceeds every NYC analog: DOT 10.0% (historical 8.6%), DOHMH 9.3% (11.3%), DPR 1.7% (4.5%), DSNY ~0%, FDNY 1.4%. Attrition rose from 19,080 (pre-pandemic YTD) to 25,966 (FY2023) before easing to 21,503 (FY2024); FDNY attrition ran +52% above pre-pandemic — mirroring Greenfield's Fire OT problem. Citywide OT spend reached $1.8B through March 2024 versus $1.1B three years earlier, with OT rising from 7.0% to 10.8% of payroll; FDNY's Fire Extinguishment division OT share hit 40.3% (from 28.9%) — the same structural pattern Greenfield sees locally (Fire 14.6%, all 12 months above threshold). NYC's remedy — centralized, faster civil-service processing (DCAS exam turnaround cut from 318 to 169 days) — is the evidence base for Proposal B's centralized hiring unit.

3.2 Service-delivery benchmarks (NYC MMR). [table]

- MMR table rows:
- DOT pothole repair % meeting time-to-close standard (30 days): 100% vs 98% target
- DOHMH food establishment inspection SLA: 90% vs 90%
- DOHMH birth certificate avg response: 2.6 days vs 3.0 target
- FDNY EMS life-threatening response: 9:32 vs 6:55 target (miss)
- FDNY structural fire response: 4:37 vs 4:14 (miss)
- DPR rec center attendance 15,808/mo; DSNY paper recycling revenue $13/ton

Lessons: (i) large agencies can sustain near-perfect performance on routine, well-staffed processes (potholes) even amid citywide stress; (ii) response-time services degrade when staffing tightens (FDNY EMS misses) — relevant to Greenfield Fire's OT dependence; (iii) NYC benchmarks are useful directional context but Greenfield's budget-per-employee runs at 4–18% of NYC analogs (Table 3), so NYC-scale solutions must be scaled to Greenfield's capacity.

3.3 Per-employee budget comparison (Table 3) — NYC FY2024 modified budgets ÷ OSC headcounts vs Greenfield (payroll+OT ÷ filled): ratios 0.108 (Parks), 0.086 (Sanitation), 0.064 (Transportation), 0.041 (Health), 0.184 (Fire). Caveat: NYC figures include fringe and OTPS; used directionally to size programs, not as parity targets.

4. Proposal A — "Consolidate" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: Health + Parks → Community Wellness (212 auth / 190 filled / 22 vac, 10.4%; OT $979,350 at blended $36.78/hr); Sanitation + Transportation → Public Works (242 / 215 / 27, 11.2%; OT $1,289,856 at $32.76/hr); Fire unchanged.

(a) Process bottlenecks. A relies on shared management spans and consolidated back offices to release 4 duplicated administrative FTE ($85,000 loaded each = $340,000). It does not touch the manual-process bottleneck: the eight below-threshold processes remain below threshold; modeled average SLA lift is +2.9 points, reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 6. Street Resurfacing (48.3%) and Plan Review (59.6%) see zero modeled lift.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Modeled savings: Public Works OT −10% ($128,986) and Community Wellness OT −5% ($48,968). But the merger does not touch Fire — 47.9% of citywide OT — and blends lower-rate Parks hours ($32.50) with higher-rate Health hours ($41.50), diluting the weighted rate. The 10% PW reduction assumes routing flexibility across Sanitation and Transportation that the current collective-bargaining and licensing distinctions do not yet support (assumption A-5).

(c) Service-delivery risk. Merging two 311 intake categories and two service catalogs risks a transition dip: NYC's experience with agency mergers (e.g., DOHMH formation) shows 12–18 months of process re-stabilization. Greenfield's model carries forward current-cycle times; the 63 open 311 requests and 44 over-30-day cases would transfer to new queue ownership mid-stream. Health's high-priority response (13.9 days, worst in city) inherits Parks' lower-rate staffing pool — a quality risk for time-critical public-health work.

(d) Workforce feasibility. The four de-dup FTE must come from somewhere — attrition timing is not guaranteed; forced reductions in a 9.1%-vacancy labor market would compound the attrition problem (NYC lost 25,966 workers in FY2023 alone). Vacancy concentration is unchanged: the two merged departments would hold 49 of the city's 54 vacancies, with Public Works at 11.2% and Community Wellness at 10.4% — closer to, not below, trigger levels.

Financials: annual savings $517,954; one-time implementation $150,000; Year-1 net +$108,977 (50% realization assumed on savings).

5. Proposal B — "Targeted Fix" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: retain five departments; (i) centralized hiring unit (2 HR FTE, $150,000/yr) covering the eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger (230 auth, 36 vac, 15.7%); (ii) 20 targeted hires (12 Transportation, 8 Health) plus 5 Fire position fills; (iii) 40-person cross-training pool (12 Parks, 14 Sanitation, 14 Transportation) with shared OT budget authority for departments above the 10% OT threshold.

(a) Process bottlenecks. B's SLA lift is modeled at +6.9 points on the eight red processes (e.g., Street Resurfacing +10 to 58.3%; Illegal Dumping +8 to 62.2%), reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 3 — the largest of any option — by adding field capacity where the backlogs are. Residual red processes (and the manual-process finding generally) require the automation triage in §7.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Savings are built from the actual trigger evidence: Sanitation OT −$97,032 and Parks OT −$45,396 from cross-training capacity ($142,428; the complementary seasonal cycles make the pool productive year-round); Fire: 5 fills absorb 7,500 excess OT hours ($360,000 avoided at $48.00/hr) against $328,665 of in-budget payroll reallocation, plus $189,563 of scheduling-driven reduction (29% of residual excess hours), leaving a $104,112 residual to manage into FY2026. Fire's structural excess (13,618 hours, $653,664) is directly addressed — Proposal A leaves it untouched.

(c) Service-delivery risk. Lowest of the options: no department boundaries change, 311 queue ownership is stable, and the hires land in exactly the divisions with the worst SLAs (all four Transportation divisions, all four Health divisions). Modeled citywide 311 average improves from 10.8 to 9.5 days. Risk concentrates in hiring-market feasibility — 20 competitive hires in a tight market — mitigated by the centralized unit and phased onboarding (assumption B-3).

(d) Workforce feasibility. Vacancy falls from 9.1% to 4.9% (Transportation 6.0%, Health 8.3%, Fire 0.0%) — at or below NYC analogs (DOT 10.0%, DOHMH 9.3%). 27 FTE are reallocated (20 hires + 5 fills + 2 HR). Turnover in the target divisions runs 15.2–26.1%, so sustained vacancy relief requires the retention elements (cross-training, scheduling relief) — which B funds.

Financials: gross OT savings $691,991; net annual savings $531,991 (after $160,000 annual program cost); one-time cost $224,000 ($160,000 recruiting at $8,000/hire + $64,000 training at $1,600 each); Year-1 net +$41,996; capacity converted to regular time $1,395,941.

6. Comparative Assessment

7. Recommendation

Adopt Proposal B as the primary framework, with two supplements and one guardrail:

1. B framework (centralized hiring + targeted hires/fills + cross-training + shared OT budget): net annual $531,991; Yr-1 net +$41,996; vacancy 9.1%→4.9%; SLA lift +6.9; red processes 8→3.
2. 3. Automation triage: commission a 90-day process-automation assessment of the eight manual, below-65% processes (all 8 red processes are Manual; Manual avg 63.6% on-time vs Automated 94.8%). 4. Guardrail: 12-month review gate. Council reconvenes on measured vacancy rate, OT share of regular hours, on-time SLA compliance, and 311 backlog before FY2027 budget adoption; unused hiring appropriation lapses if milestone SLAs are not met.

MEMO

TO: Members of the City Council, City of Greenfield
FROM: Office of Management and Budget — Management Analysis Unit
DATE: October 19, 2026
RE: Departmental Restructuring Decision — Analysis of Proposal A (Consolidation) and Proposal B (Targeted Fix), with Recommended Hybrid Approach

1. Purpose and Recommendation Summary

This memorandum presents the cost-benefit analysis supporting the Council's upcoming vote on the departmental restructuring. Two proposals were modeled against the FY2024 baseline:

- Proposal A ("Consolidate") merges Health Services and Parks & Recreation into a Community Wellness department, and Sanitation and Transportation into a Public Works department; Fire remains standalone.
- Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") retains all five departments and adds a centralized hiring unit for high-vacancy divisions, cross-training pools, and shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding a 10% overtime-to-regular-hours threshold.

Recommended action: Adopt Proposal B as the primary operating framework, supplemented by (i) a voluntary Sanitation–Transportation "Shared Fleet & Routing Compact" that captures the interdepartmental coordination benefit Proposal A sought through full merger, without the governance risk, and (ii) an automation triage program targeting the eight manual, below-threshold processes. Head-to-head, Proposal B produces marginally higher annual savings ($531,991 vs $517,954), nearly seven times the service-delivery improvement (SLA lift +6.9 vs +2.9 points; below-threshold processes reduced from 8 to 3 vs 8 to 6), a lower implementation risk rating (2 vs 3 on a 5-point scale), and a materially larger workforce stabilization effect (27 FTE reallocated vs 4). A weighted net score (savings 25%, SLA improvement 30%, complexity 20%, risk 25%) yields 2.89 for B versus 1.81 for A.

2. Situation Overview: Staffing Health and Service Outcomes

2.1 Workforce position. Greenfield's five operating departments are authorized for 596 positions; 542 are filled, leaving 54 vacancies (9.1%). Payroll is $28.39M; overtime adds $4.35M (9.6% of 1,141,177 regular hours), for total personnel cost of $32.74M.

Table 1 — FY2024 department scorecard (red flags: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%)

[table]

Three findings stand out:

1. Vacancy is concentrated, not evenly distributed. All eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger are in Transportation (14.8–15.8% by division) and Health Services (13.6–18.2%); together these divisions hold 230 authorized positions and 36 vacancies (15.7%). Transportation's 14.9% departmental vacancy rate and Health's 16.7% are the direct drivers of the citywide 9.1%.
2. Overtime is a Fire Department problem first. Fire accounts for 47.9% of citywide OT spend ($2.09M of $4.35M) at the highest rate in the workforce ($48.00/hr) and exceeded the 10% OT-to-regular-hours threshold in all 12 months of FY2024. Sanitation sits on the watchlist (9.8% annual, but above 10% in four winter months — 52.9% of its annual OT falls in November–March, $342,302), while Parks is summer-concentrated (44.6% of its OT in May–August, $202,540). The two seasonal patterns are complementary — an argument for cross-training rather than merger.
3. Service outcomes track staffing health. Transportation has the worst 311 performance (13.6-day average resolution; 45.2-day Street Resurfacing cycle against a 30-day target; 48.3% on-time) and the lowest satisfaction (3.36/5.0). Health Services' high-priority requests average 13.9 days — the worst in the city. Citywide, of 500 FY2024 311 requests, 437 closed and 63 remain open; the weighted average resolution is 10.8 days; 44 requests (10.1%) exceeded 30 days; weighted satisfaction is 3.63/5.0.

2.4 The cross-cutting bottleneck is automation, not structure. Of 25 mapped processes, the 8 below the 65% on-time threshold are all Manual. Manual processes average 63.6% on-time, 5.9% error, and 16.1-day cycles; Semi-Automated average 80.8% / 3.7% / 4.1 days; Automated 94.8% / 1.4% / 1.1 days. Neither proposal as written addresses this gap (see Recommendation, §7).

3. NYC Benchmark Context

3.1 Staffing trends (NYS Comptroller, Report 2-2025). New York City's post-pandemic experience frames Greenfield's choices. Citywide vacancy peaked at 8.4% (Dec 2022) and stood at 5.1% in January 2024 — still 2.5x the pre-pandemic 2.0%. Greenfield's 9.1% exceeds every NYC analog: DOT 10.0% (historical 8.6%), DOHMH 9.3% (11.3%), DPR 1.7% (4.5%), DSNY ~0%, FDNY 1.4%. Attrition rose from 19,080 (pre-pandemic YTD) to 25,966 (FY2023) before easing to 21,503 (FY2024); FDNY attrition ran +52% above pre-pandemic — mirroring Greenfield's Fire OT problem. Citywide OT spend reached $1.8B through March 2024 versus $1.1B three years earlier, with OT rising from 7.0% to 10.8% of payroll; FDNY's Fire Extinguishment division OT share hit 40.3% (from 28.9%) — the same structural pattern Greenfield sees locally (Fire 14.6%, all 12 months above threshold). NYC's remedy — centralized, faster civil-service processing (DCAS exam turnaround cut from 318 to 169 days) — is the evidence base for Proposal B's centralized hiring unit.

3.2 Service-delivery benchmarks (NYC MMR). [table]

- MMR table rows:
- DOT pothole repair % meeting time-to-close standard (30 days): 100% vs 98% target
- DOHMH food establishment inspection SLA: 90% vs 90%
- DOHMH birth certificate avg response: 2.6 days vs 3.0 target
- FDNY EMS life-threatening response: 9:32 vs 6:55 target (miss)
- FDNY structural fire response: 4:37 vs 4:14 (miss)
- DPR rec center attendance 15,808/mo; DSNY paper recycling revenue $13/ton

Lessons: (i) large agencies can sustain near-perfect performance on routine, well-staffed processes (potholes) even amid citywide stress; (ii) response-time services degrade when staffing tightens (FDNY EMS misses) — relevant to Greenfield Fire's OT dependence; (iii) NYC benchmarks are useful directional context but Greenfield's budget-per-employee runs at 4–18% of NYC analogs (Table 3), so NYC-scale solutions must be scaled to Greenfield's capacity.

3.3 Per-employee budget comparison (Table 3) — NYC FY2024 modified budgets ÷ OSC headcounts vs Greenfield (payroll+OT ÷ filled): ratios 0.108 (Parks), 0.086 (Sanitation), 0.064 (Transportation), 0.041 (Health), 0.184 (Fire). Caveat: NYC figures include fringe and OTPS; used directionally to size programs, not as parity targets.

4. Proposal A — "Consolidate" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: Health + Parks → Community Wellness (212 auth / 190 filled / 22 vac, 10.4%; OT $979,350 at blended $36.78/hr); Sanitation + Transportation → Public Works (242 / 215 / 27, 11.2%; OT $1,289,856 at $32.76/hr); Fire unchanged.

(a) Process bottlenecks. A relies on shared management spans and consolidated back offices to release 4 duplicated administrative FTE ($85,000 loaded each = $340,000). It does not touch the manual-process bottleneck: the eight below-threshold processes remain below threshold; modeled average SLA lift is +2.9 points, reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 6. Street Resurfacing (48.3%) and Plan Review (59.6%) see zero modeled lift.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Modeled savings: Public Works OT −10% ($128,986) and Community Wellness OT −5% ($48,968). But the merger does not touch Fire — 47.9% of citywide OT — and blends lower-rate Parks hours ($32.50) with higher-rate Health hours ($41.50), diluting the weighted rate. The 10% PW reduction assumes routing flexibility across Sanitation and Transportation that the current collective-bargaining and licensing distinctions do not yet support (assumption A-5).

(c) Service-delivery risk. Merging two 311 intake categories and two service catalogs risks a transition dip: NYC's experience with agency mergers (e.g., DOHMH formation) shows 12–18 months of process re-stabilization. Greenfield's model carries forward current-cycle times; the 63 open 311 requests and 44 over-30-day cases would transfer to new queue ownership mid-stream. Health's high-priority response (13.9 days, worst in city) inherits Parks' lower-rate staffing pool — a quality risk for time-critical public-health work.

(d) Workforce feasibility. The four de-dup FTE must come from somewhere — attrition timing is not guaranteed; forced reductions in a 9.1%-vacancy labor market would compound the attrition problem (NYC lost 25,966 workers in FY2023 alone). Vacancy concentration is unchanged: the two merged departments would hold 49 of the city's 54 vacancies, with Public Works at 11.2% and Community Wellness at 10.4% — closer to, not below, trigger levels.

Financials: annual savings $517,954; one-time implementation $150,000; Year-1 net +$108,977 (50% realization assumed on savings).

5. Proposal B — "Targeted Fix" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: retain five departments; (i) centralized hiring unit (2 HR FTE, $150,000/yr) covering the eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger (230 auth, 36 vac, 15.7%); (ii) 20 targeted hires (12 Transportation, 8 Health) plus 5 Fire position fills; (iii) 40-person cross-training pool (12 Parks, 14 Sanitation, 14 Transportation) with shared OT budget authority for departments above the 10% OT threshold.

(a) Process bottlenecks. B's SLA lift is modeled at +6.9 points on the eight red processes (e.g., Street Resurfacing +10 to 58.3%; Illegal Dumping +8 to 62.2%), reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 3 — the largest of any option — by adding field capacity where the backlogs are. Residual red processes (and the manual-process finding generally) require the automation triage in §7.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Savings are built from the actual trigger evidence: Sanitation OT −$97,032 and Parks OT −$45,396 from cross-training capacity ($142,428; the complementary seasonal cycles make the pool productive year-round); Fire: 5 fills absorb 7,500 excess OT hours ($360,000 avoided at $48.00/hr) against $328,665 of in-budget payroll reallocation, plus $189,563 of scheduling-driven reduction (29% of residual excess hours), leaving a $104,112 residual to manage into FY2026. Fire's structural excess (13,618 hours, $653,664) is directly addressed — Proposal A leaves it untouched.

(c) Service-delivery risk. Lowest of the options: no department boundaries change, 311 queue ownership is stable, and the hires land in exactly the divisions with the worst SLAs (all four Transportation divisions, all four Health divisions). Modeled citywide 311 average improves from 10.8 to 9.5 days. Risk concentrates in hiring-market feasibility — 20 competitive hires in a tight market — mitigated by the centralized unit and phased onboarding (assumption B-3).

(d) Workforce feasibility. Vacancy falls from 9.1% to 4.9% (Transportation 6.0%, Health 8.3%, Fire 0.0%) — at or below NYC analogs (DOT 10.0%, DOHMH 9.3%). 27 FTE are reallocated (20 hires + 5 fills + 2 HR). Turnover in the target divisions runs 15.2–26.1%, so sustained vacancy relief requires the retention elements (cross-training, scheduling relief) — which B funds.

7. Recommendation

Adopt Proposal B as the primary framework, with two supplements and one guardrail:

1. B framework (centralized hiring + targeted hires/fills + cross-training + shared OT budget): net annual $531,991; Yr-1 net +$41,996; vacancy 9.1%→4.9%; SLA lift +6.9; red processes 8→3.
2. 4. Guardrail: 12-month review gate. Council reconvenes on measured vacancy rate, OT share of regular hours, on-time SLA compliance, and 311 backlog before FY2027 budget adoption; unused hiring appropriation lapses if milestone SLAs are not met.

## Goal

Act as a Management Analyst for the City of Greenfield (5 departments: Parks & Recreation, Sanitation, Transportation, Health Services, Fire Department — 596 authorized / 542 filled positions) and produce a **three-deliverable decision package** for City Council on a departmental restructuring vote:

1. **Decision Briefing Memo (.docx, 6–10 pages)** — situation overview (staffing health × service outcomes), NYC benchmark analysis, evaluation of both proposals on four lenses (process bottlenecks, OT cost structure, SLA service-delivery risk, workforce feasibility), clear recommendation (one proposal or defined hybrid) with quantitative arguments and explicit assumptions.
2. **Cost-Benefit Analysis Workbook (.xlsx, 4 tabs)** — "Baseline Metrics" (dept scorecard w/ red conditional formatting: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%), "Proposal A Model", "Proposal B Model", "Comparison Summary" (5 dimensions + net recommendation score).
3. **Council Presentation (.pptx, 8–12 slides)** — operational health, trade-offs, NYC benchmark context, recommendation + next steps.

All quantitative claims must be **internally consistent across all three deliverables and traceable to source data**.

## Instructions

- Proposals: **A ("Consolidate")** = merge Health+Parks → "Community Wellness", Transportation+Sanitation → "Public Works", Fire standalone; **B ("Targeted Fix")** = keep 5 departments, add cross-training pools, shared OT budgets for depts >10% OT-to-regular-hours, centralized hiring for divisions >12% vacancy.
- NYC benchmarks required: **MMR indicators (NYC Open Data rbed-zzin)** for DPR/DSNY/DOT/DOHMH/FDNY (SLA & response-time metrics) + **NYS Comptroller "2024 Update on NYC Staffing Trends" (Report 2-2025)** (post-pandemic vacancies, attrition, OT growth).
- Use pinned reference files in `/work/task_folder/references/` (no internet). Write deliverables to `/work/output/`.
- Environment constraint: **no matplotlib, no pip installs** — use openpyxl native charts for xlsx and python-pptx native charts (`shapes.add_chart` + `CategoryChartData`) for pptx. Python 3.12 with pandas, openpyxl, python-docx, python-pptx, pdfplumber, numpy available.

MEMO

TO: Members of the City Council, City of Greenfield
FROM: Office of Management and Budget — Management Analysis Unit
DATE: October 19, 2026
RE: Departmental Restructuring Decision — Analysis of Proposal A (Consolidation) and Proposal B (Targeted Fix), with Recommended Hybrid Approach

1. Purpose and Recommendation Summary

This memorandum presents the cost-benefit analysis supporting the Council's upcoming vote on the departmental restructuring. Two proposals were modeled against the FY2024 baseline:

- Proposal A ("Consolidate") merges Health Services and Parks & Recreation into a Community Wellness department, and Sanitation and Transportation into a Public Works department; Fire remains standalone.
- Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") retains all five departments and adds a centralized hiring unit for high-vacancy divisions, cross-training pools, and shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding a 10% overtime-to-regular-hours threshold.

Recommended action: Adopt Proposal B as the primary operating framework, supplemented by (i) a voluntary Sanitation–Transportation "Shared Fleet & Routing Compact" that captures the interdepartmental coordination benefit Proposal A sought through full merger, without the governance risk, and (ii) an automation triage program targeting the eight manual, below-threshold processes. Head-to-head, Proposal B produces marginally higher annual savings ($531,991 vs $517,954), nearly seven times the service-delivery improvement (SLA lift +6.9 vs +2.9 points; below-threshold processes reduced from 8 to 3 vs 8 to 6), a lower implementation risk rating (2 vs 3 on a 5-point scale), and a materially larger workforce stabilization effect (27 FTE reallocated vs 4). A weighted net score (savings 25%, SLA improvement 30%, complexity 20%, risk 25%) yields 2.89 for B versus 1.81 for A.

2. Situation Overview: Staffing Health and Service Outcomes

2.1 Workforce position. Greenfield's five operating departments are authorized for 596 positions; 542 are filled, leaving 54 vacancies (9.1%). Payroll is $28.39M; overtime adds $4.35M (9.6% of 1,141,177 regular hours), for total personnel cost of $32.74M.

Table 1 — FY2024 department scorecard (red flags: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%)

[table]

Three findings stand out:

1. Vacancy is concentrated, not evenly distributed. All eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger are in Transportation (14.8–15.8% by division) and Health Services (13.6–18.2%); together these divisions hold 230 authorized positions and 36 vacancies (15.7%). Transportation's 14.9% departmental vacancy rate and Health's 16.7% are the direct drivers of the citywide 9.1%.
2. Overtime is a Fire Department problem first. Fire accounts for 47.9% of citywide OT spend ($2.09M of $4.35M) at the highest rate in the workforce ($48.00/hr) and exceeded the 10% OT-to-regular-hours threshold in all 12 months of FY2024. Sanitation sits on the watchlist (9.8% annual, but above 10% in four winter months — 52.9% of its annual OT falls in November–March, $342,302), while Parks is summer-concentrated (44.6% of its OT in May–August, $202,540). The two seasonal patterns are complementary — an argument for cross-training rather than merger.
3. Service outcomes track staffing health. Transportation has the worst 311 performance (13.6-day average resolution; 45.2-day Street Resurfacing cycle against a 30-day target; 48.3% on-time) and the lowest satisfaction (3.36/5.0). Health Services' high-priority requests average 13.9 days — the worst in the city. Citywide, of 500 FY2024 311 requests, 437 closed and 63 remain open; the weighted average resolution is 10.8 days; 44 requests (10.1%) exceeded 30 days; weighted satisfaction is 3.63/5.0.

2.4 The cross-cutting bottleneck is automation, not structure. Of 25 mapped processes, the 8 below the 65% on-time threshold are all Manual. Manual processes average 63.6% on-time, 5.9% error, and 16.1-day cycles; Semi-Automated average 80.8% / 3.7% / 4.1 days; Automated 94.8% / 1.4% / 1.1 days. Neither proposal as written addresses this gap (see Recommendation, §7).

3. NYC Benchmark Context

3.1 Staffing trends (NYS Comptroller, Report 2-2025). New York City's post-pandemic experience frames Greenfield's choices. Citywide vacancy peaked at 8.4% (Dec 2022) and stood at 5.1% in January 2024 — still 2.5x the pre-pandemic 2.0%. Greenfield's 9.1% exceeds every NYC analog: DOT 10.0% (historical 8.6%), DOHMH 9.3% (11.3%), DPR 1.7% (4.5%), DSNY ~0%, FDNY 1.4%. Attrition rose from 19,080 (pre-pandemic YTD) to 25,966 (FY2023) before easing to 21,503 (FY2024); FDNY attrition ran +52% above pre-pandemic — mirroring Greenfield's Fire OT problem. Citywide OT spend reached $1.8B through March 2024 versus $1.1B three years earlier, with OT rising from 7.0% to 10.8% of payroll; FDNY's Fire Extinguishment division OT share hit 40.3% (from 28.9%) — the same structural pattern Greenfield sees locally (Fire 14.6%, all 12 months above threshold). NYC's remedy — centralized, faster civil-service processing (DCAS exam turnaround cut from 318 to 169 days) — is the evidence base for Proposal B's centralized hiring unit.

3.2 Service-delivery benchmarks (NYC MMR). [table]

- MMR table rows:
- DOT pothole repair % meeting time-to-close standard (30 days): 100% vs 98% target
- DOHMH food establishment inspection SLA: 90% vs 90%
- DOHMH birth certificate avg response: 2.6 days vs 3.0 target
- FDNY EMS life-threatening response: 9:32 vs 6:55 target (miss)
- FDNY structural fire response: 4:37 vs 4:14 (miss)
- DPR rec center attendance 15,808/mo; DSNY paper recycling revenue $13/ton

Lessons: (i) large agencies can sustain near-perfect performance on routine, well-staffed processes (potholes) even amid citywide stress; (ii) response-time services degrade when staffing tightens (FDNY EMS misses) — relevant to Greenfield Fire's OT dependence; (iii) NYC benchmarks are useful directional context but Greenfield's budget-per-employee runs at 4–18% of NYC analogs (Table 3), so NYC-scale solutions must be scaled to Greenfield's capacity.

3.3 Per-employee budget comparison (Table 3) — NYC FY2024 modified budgets ÷ OSC headcounts vs Greenfield (payroll+OT ÷ filled): ratios 0.108 (Parks), 0.086 (Sanitation), 0.064 (Transportation), 0.041 (Health), 0.184 (Fire). Caveat: NYC figures include fringe and OTPS; used directionally to size programs, not as parity targets.

4. Proposal A — "Consolidate" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: Health + Parks → Community Wellness (212 auth / 190 filled / 22 vac, 10.4%; OT $979,350 at blended $36.78/hr); Sanitation + Transportation → Public Works (242 / 215 / 27, 11.2%; OT $1,289,856 at $32.76/hr); Fire unchanged.

(a) Process bottlenecks. A relies on shared management spans and consolidated back offices to release 4 duplicated administrative FTE ($85,000 loaded each = $340,000). It does not touch the manual-process bottleneck: the eight below-threshold processes remain below threshold; modeled average SLA lift is +2.9 points, reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 6. Street Resurfacing (48.3%) and Plan Review (59.6%) see zero modeled lift.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Modeled savings: Public Works OT −10% ($128,986) and Community Wellness OT −5% ($48,968). But the merger does not touch Fire — 47.9% of citywide OT — and blends lower-rate Parks hours ($32.50) with higher-rate Health hours ($41.50), diluting the weighted rate. The 10% PW reduction assumes routing flexibility across Sanitation and Transportation that the current collective-bargaining and licensing distinctions do not yet support (assumption A-5).

(c) Service-delivery risk. Merging two 311 intake categories and two service catalogs risks a transition dip: NYC's experience with agency mergers (e.g., DOHMH formation) shows 12–18 months of process re-stabilization. Greenfield's model carries forward current-cycle times; the 63 open 311 requests and 44 over-30-day cases would transfer to new queue ownership mid-stream. Health's high-priority response (13.9 days, worst in city) inherits Parks' lower-rate staffing pool — a quality risk for time-critical public-health work.

(d) Workforce feasibility. The four de-dup FTE must come from somewhere — attrition timing is not guaranteed; forced reductions in a 9.1%-vacancy labor market would compound the attrition problem (NYC lost 25,966 workers in FY2023 alone). Vacancy concentration is unchanged: the two merged departments would hold 49 of the city's 54 vacancies, with Public Works at 11.2% and Community Wellness at 10.4% — closer to, not below, trigger levels.

Financials: annual savings $517,954; one-time implementation $150,000; Year-1 net +$108,977 (50% realization assumed on savings).

5. Proposal B — "Targeted Fix" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: retain five departments; (i) centralized hiring unit (2 HR FTE, $150,000/yr) covering the eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger (230 auth, 36 vac, 15.7%); (ii) 20 targeted hires (12 Transportation, 8 Health) plus 5 Fire position fills; (iii) 40-person cross-training pool (12 Parks, 14 Sanitation, 14 Transportation) with shared OT budget authority for departments above the 10% OT threshold.

(a) Process bottlenecks. B's SLA lift is modeled at +6.9 points on the eight red processes (e.g., Street Resurfacing +10 to 58.3%; Illegal Dumping +8 to 62.2%), reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 3 — the largest of any option — by adding field capacity where the backlogs are. Residual red processes (and the manual-process finding generally) require the automation triage in §7.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Savings are built from the actual trigger evidence: Sanitation OT −$97,032 and Parks OT −$45,396 from cross-training capacity ($142,428; the complementary seasonal cycles make the pool productive year-round); Fire: 5 fills absorb 7,500 excess OT hours ($360,000 avoided at $48.00/hr) against $328,665 of in-budget payroll reallocation, plus $189,563 of scheduling-driven reduction (29% of residual excess hours), leaving a $104,112 residual to manage into FY2026. Fire's structural excess (13,618 hours, $653,664) is directly addressed — Proposal A leaves it untouched.

(c) Service-delivery risk. Lowest of the options: no department boundaries change, 311 queue ownership is stable, and the hires land in exactly the divisions with the worst SLAs (all four Transportation divisions, all four Health divisions). Modeled citywide 311 average improves from 10.8 to 9.5 days. Risk concentrates in hiring-market feasibility — 20 competitive hires in a tight market — mitigated by the centralized unit and phased onboarding (assumption B-3).

(d) Workforce feasibility. Vacancy falls from 9.1% to 4.9% (Transportation 6.0%, Health 8.3%, Fire 0.0%) — at or below NYC analogs (DOT 10.0%, DOHMH 9.3%). 27 FTE are reallocated (20 hires + 5 fills + 2 HR). Turnover in the target divisions runs 15.2–26.1%, so sustained vacancy relief requires the retention elements (cross-training, scheduling relief) — which B funds.

Financials: gross OT savings $691,991; net annual savings $531,991 (after $160,000 annual program cost); one-time cost $224,000 ($160,000 recruiting at $8,000/hire + $64,000 training at $1,600 each); Year-1 net +$41,996; capacity converted to regular time $1,395,941.

6. Comparative Assessment

7. Recommendation

Adopt Proposal B as the primary framework, with two supplements and one guardrail:

1. B framework (centralized hiring + targeted hires/fills + cross-training + shared OT budget): net annual $531,991; Yr-1 net +$41,996; vacancy 9.1%→4.9%; SLA lift +6.9; red processes 8→3.
2. 3. Automation triage: commission a 90-day process-automation assessment of the eight manual, below-65% processes (all 8 red processes are Manual; Manual avg 63.6% on-time vs Automated 94.8%). 4. Guardrail: 12-month review gate. Council reconvenes on measured vacancy rate, OT share of regular hours, on-time SLA compliance, and 311 backlog before FY2027 budget adoption; unused hiring appropriation lapses if milestone SLAs are not met.

MEMO

TO: Members of the City Council, City of Greenfield
FROM: Office of Management and Budget — Management Analysis Unit
DATE: October 19, 2026
RE: Departmental Restructuring Decision — Analysis of Proposal A (Consolidation) and Proposal B (Targeted Fix), with Recommended Hybrid Approach

1. Purpose and Recommendation Summary

This memorandum presents the cost-benefit analysis supporting the Council's upcoming vote on the departmental restructuring. Two proposals were modeled against the FY2024 baseline:

- Proposal A ("Consolidate") merges Health Services and Parks & Recreation into a Community Wellness department, and Sanitation and Transportation into a Public Works department; Fire remains standalone.
- Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") retains all five departments and adds a centralized hiring unit for high-vacancy divisions, cross-training pools, and shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding a 10% overtime-to-regular-hours threshold.

Recommended action: Adopt Proposal B as the primary operating framework, supplemented by (i) a voluntary Sanitation–Transportation "Shared Fleet & Routing Compact" that captures the interdepartmental coordination benefit Proposal A sought through full merger, without the governance risk, and (ii) an automation triage program targeting the eight manual, below-threshold processes. Head-to-head, Proposal B produces marginally higher annual savings ($531,991 vs $517,954), nearly seven times the service-delivery improvement (SLA lift +6.9 vs +2.9 points; below-threshold processes reduced from 8 to 3 vs 8 to 6), a lower implementation risk rating (2 vs 3 on a 5-point scale), and a materially larger workforce stabilization effect (27 FTE reallocated vs 4). A weighted net score (savings 25%, SLA improvement 30%, complexity 20%, risk 25%) yields 2.89 for B versus 1.81 for A.

2. Situation Overview: Staffing Health and Service Outcomes

2.1 Workforce position. Greenfield's five operating departments are authorized for 596 positions; 542 are filled, leaving 54 vacancies (9.1%). Payroll is $28.39M; overtime adds $4.35M (9.6% of 1,141,177 regular hours), for total personnel cost of $32.74M.

Table 1 — FY2024 department scorecard (red flags: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%)

[table]

Three findings stand out:

1. Vacancy is concentrated, not evenly distributed. All eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger are in Transportation (14.8–15.8% by division) and Health Services (13.6–18.2%); together these divisions hold 230 authorized positions and 36 vacancies (15.7%). Transportation's 14.9% departmental vacancy rate and Health's 16.7% are the direct drivers of the citywide 9.1%.
2. Overtime is a Fire Department problem first. Fire accounts for 47.9% of citywide OT spend ($2.09M of $4.35M) at the highest rate in the workforce ($48.00/hr) and exceeded the 10% OT-to-regular-hours threshold in all 12 months of FY2024. Sanitation sits on the watchlist (9.8% annual, but above 10% in four winter months — 52.9% of its annual OT falls in November–March, $342,302), while Parks is summer-concentrated (44.6% of its OT in May–August, $202,540). The two seasonal patterns are complementary — an argument for cross-training rather than merger.
3. Service outcomes track staffing health. Transportation has the worst 311 performance (13.6-day average resolution; 45.2-day Street Resurfacing cycle against a 30-day target; 48.3% on-time) and the lowest satisfaction (3.36/5.0). Health Services' high-priority requests average 13.9 days — the worst in the city. Citywide, of 500 FY2024 311 requests, 437 closed and 63 remain open; the weighted average resolution is 10.8 days; 44 requests (10.1%) exceeded 30 days; weighted satisfaction is 3.63/5.0.

2.4 The cross-cutting bottleneck is automation, not structure. Of 25 mapped processes, the 8 below the 65% on-time threshold are all Manual. Manual processes average 63.6% on-time, 5.9% error, and 16.1-day cycles; Semi-Automated average 80.8% / 3.7% / 4.1 days; Automated 94.8% / 1.4% / 1.1 days. Neither proposal as written addresses this gap (see Recommendation, §7).

3. NYC Benchmark Context

3.1 Staffing trends (NYS Comptroller, Report 2-2025). New York City's post-pandemic experience frames Greenfield's choices. Citywide vacancy peaked at 8.4% (Dec 2022) and stood at 5.1% in January 2024 — still 2.5x the pre-pandemic 2.0%. Greenfield's 9.1% exceeds every NYC analog: DOT 10.0% (historical 8.6%), DOHMH 9.3% (11.3%), DPR 1.7% (4.5%), DSNY ~0%, FDNY 1.4%. Attrition rose from 19,080 (pre-pandemic YTD) to 25,966 (FY2023) before easing to 21,503 (FY2024); FDNY attrition ran +52% above pre-pandemic — mirroring Greenfield's Fire OT problem. Citywide OT spend reached $1.8B through March 2024 versus $1.1B three years earlier, with OT rising from 7.0% to 10.8% of payroll; FDNY's Fire Extinguishment division OT share hit 40.3% (from 28.9%) — the same structural pattern Greenfield sees locally (Fire 14.6%, all 12 months above threshold). NYC's remedy — centralized, faster civil-service processing (DCAS exam turnaround cut from 318 to 169 days) — is the evidence base for Proposal B's centralized hiring unit.

3.2 Service-delivery benchmarks (NYC MMR). [table]

- MMR table rows:
- DOT pothole repair % meeting time-to-close standard (30 days): 100% vs 98% target
- DOHMH food establishment inspection SLA: 90% vs 90%
- DOHMH birth certificate avg response: 2.6 days vs 3.0 target
- FDNY EMS life-threatening response: 9:32 vs 6:55 target (miss)
- FDNY structural fire response: 4:37 vs 4:14 (miss)
- DPR rec center attendance 15,808/mo; DSNY paper recycling revenue $13/ton

Lessons: (i) large agencies can sustain near-perfect performance on routine, well-staffed processes (potholes) even amid citywide stress; (ii) response-time services degrade when staffing tightens (FDNY EMS misses) — relevant to Greenfield Fire's OT dependence; (iii) NYC benchmarks are useful directional context but Greenfield's budget-per-employee runs at 4–18% of NYC analogs (Table 3), so NYC-scale solutions must be scaled to Greenfield's capacity.

3.3 Per-employee budget comparison (Table 3) — NYC FY2024 modified budgets ÷ OSC headcounts vs Greenfield (payroll+OT ÷ filled): ratios 0.108 (Parks), 0.086 (Sanitation), 0.064 (Transportation), 0.041 (Health), 0.184 (Fire). Caveat: NYC figures include fringe and OTPS; used directionally to size programs, not as parity targets.

4. Proposal A — "Consolidate" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: Health + Parks → Community Wellness (212 auth / 190 filled / 22 vac, 10.4%; OT $979,350 at blended $36.78/hr); Sanitation + Transportation → Public Works (242 / 215 / 27, 11.2%; OT $1,289,856 at $32.76/hr); Fire unchanged.

(a) Process bottlenecks. A relies on shared management spans and consolidated back offices to release 4 duplicated administrative FTE ($85,000 loaded each = $340,000). It does not touch the manual-process bottleneck: the eight below-threshold processes remain below threshold; modeled average SLA lift is +2.9 points, reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 6. Street Resurfacing (48.3%) and Plan Review (59.6%) see zero modeled lift.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Modeled savings: Public Works OT −10% ($128,986) and Community Wellness OT −5% ($48,968). But the merger does not touch Fire — 47.9% of citywide OT — and blends lower-rate Parks hours ($32.50) with higher-rate Health hours ($41.50), diluting the weighted rate. The 10% PW reduction assumes routing flexibility across Sanitation and Transportation that the current collective-bargaining and licensing distinctions do not yet support (assumption A-5).

(c) Service-delivery risk. Merging two 311 intake categories and two service catalogs risks a transition dip: NYC's experience with agency mergers (e.g., DOHMH formation) shows 12–18 months of process re-stabilization. Greenfield's model carries forward current-cycle times; the 63 open 311 requests and 44 over-30-day cases would transfer to new queue ownership mid-stream. Health's high-priority response (13.9 days, worst in city) inherits Parks' lower-rate staffing pool — a quality risk for time-critical public-health work.

(d) Workforce feasibility. The four de-dup FTE must come from somewhere — attrition timing is not guaranteed; forced reductions in a 9.1%-vacancy labor market would compound the attrition problem (NYC lost 25,966 workers in FY2023 alone). Vacancy concentration is unchanged: the two merged departments would hold 49 of the city's 54 vacancies, with Public Works at 11.2% and Community Wellness at 10.4% — closer to, not below, trigger levels.

Financials: annual savings $517,954; one-time implementation $150,000; Year-1 net +$108,977 (50% realization assumed on savings).

5. Proposal B — "Targeted Fix" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: retain five departments; (i) centralized hiring unit (2 HR FTE, $150,000/yr) covering the eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger (230 auth, 36 vac, 15.7%); (ii) 20 targeted hires (12 Transportation, 8 Health) plus 5 Fire position fills; (iii) 40-person cross-training pool (12 Parks, 14 Sanitation, 14 Transportation) with shared OT budget authority for departments above the 10% OT threshold.

(a) Process bottlenecks. B's SLA lift is modeled at +6.9 points on the eight red processes (e.g., Street Resurfacing +10 to 58.3%; Illegal Dumping +8 to 62.2%), reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 3 — the largest of any option — by adding field capacity where the backlogs are. Residual red processes (and the manual-process finding generally) require the automation triage in §7.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Savings are built from the actual trigger evidence: Sanitation OT −$97,032 and Parks OT −$45,396 from cross-training capacity ($142,428; the complementary seasonal cycles make the pool productive year-round); Fire: 5 fills absorb 7,500 excess OT hours ($360,000 avoided at $48.00/hr) against $328,665 of in-budget payroll reallocation, plus $189,563 of scheduling-driven reduction (29% of residual excess hours), leaving a $104,112 residual to manage into FY2026. Fire's structural excess (13,618 hours, $653,664) is directly addressed — Proposal A leaves it untouched.

(c) Service-delivery risk. Lowest of the options: no department boundaries change, 311 queue ownership is stable, and the hires land in exactly the divisions with the worst SLAs (all four Transportation divisions, all four Health divisions). Modeled citywide 311 average improves from 10.8 to 9.5 days. Risk concentrates in hiring-market feasibility — 20 competitive hires in a tight market — mitigated by the centralized unit and phased onboarding (assumption B-3).

(d) Workforce feasibility. Vacancy falls from 9.1% to 4.9% (Transportation 6.0%, Health 8.3%, Fire 0.0%) — at or below NYC analogs (DOT 10.0%, DOHMH 9.3%). 27 FTE are reallocated (20 hires + 5 fills + 2 HR). Turnover in the target divisions runs 15.2–26.1%, so sustained vacancy relief requires the retention elements (cross-training, scheduling relief) — which B funds.

7. Recommendation

Adopt Proposal B as the primary framework, with two supplements and one guardrail:

1. B framework (centralized hiring + targeted hires/fills + cross-training + shared OT budget): net annual $531,991; Yr-1 net +$41,996; vacancy 9.1%→4.9%; SLA lift +6.9; red processes 8→3.
2. ## Goal

Act as a Management Analyst for the City of Greenfield (5 departments: Parks & Recreation, Sanitation, Transportation, Health Services, Fire Department — 596 authorized / 542 filled positions) and produce a **three-deliverable decision package** for City Council on a departmental restructuring vote:

1. **Decision Briefing Memo (.docx, 6–10 pages)** — situation overview (staffing health × service outcomes), NYC benchmark analysis, evaluation of both proposals on four lenses (process bottlenecks, OT cost structure, SLA service-delivery risk, workforce feasibility), clear recommendation (one proposal or defined hybrid) with quantitative arguments and explicit assumptions.
2. **Cost-Benefit Analysis Workbook (.xlsx, 4 tabs)** — "Baseline Metrics" (dept scorecard w/ red conditional formatting: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%), "Proposal A Model", "Proposal B Model", "Comparison Summary" (5 dimensions + net recommendation score).
3. **Council Presentation (.pptx, 8–12 slides)** — operational health, trade-offs, NYC benchmark context, recommendation + next steps.

All quantitative claims must be **internally consistent across all three deliverables and traceable to source data**.

## Instructions

- Proposals: **A ("Consolidate")** = merge Health+Parks → "Community Wellness", Transportation+Sanitation → "Public Works", Fire standalone; **B ("Targeted Fix")** = keep 5 departments, add cross-training pools, shared OT budgets for depts >10% OT-to-regular-hours, centralized hiring for divisions >12% vacancy.
- NYC benchmarks required: **MMR indicators (NYC Open Data rbed-zzin)** for DPR/DSNY/DOT/DOHMH/FDNY (SLA & response-time metrics) + **NYS Comptroller "2024 Update on NYC Staffing Trends" (Report 2-2025)** (post-pandemic vacancies, attrition, OT growth).
- Use pinned reference files in `/work/task_folder/references/` (no internet). Write deliverables to `/work/output/`.
- Environment constraint: **no matplotlib, no pip installs** — use openpyxl native charts for xlsx and python-pptx native charts (`shapes.add_chart` + `CategoryChartData`) for pptx. Python 3.12 with pandas, openpyxl, python-docx, python-pptx, pdfplumber, numpy available.

## Discoveries

**Environment:** Build scripts and a locked model live in `/work/build/`. `/work/build/master.py` + `/work/build/model2.py` computed everything into **`/work/build/model.json`** (single source of truth). The Comptroller PDF text is extracted at `/tmp/pdf_text.txt`.

**Greenfield baseline (from source files):**
- Citywide: 596 auth / 542 filled / **54 vacant (9.1%)**; payroll $28,389,900; OT $4,354,518 (**9.6%** of 1,141,177 regular hrs); personnel total $32,744,418.
- Dept scorecard: Parks 5.2% vac / OT 6.1% ($453,960) / 311 avg 12.5d / worst on-time 62.4% (Tree Removal); Sanitation 6.5% / 9.8% ($646,877) / 9.05d / 54.2% (Illegal Dumping); Transportation **14.9%** / 8.4% ($642,979) / 13.62d / 48.3% (Street Resurfacing); Health **16.7%** / 7.1% ($525,390) / 12.0d / 64.1% (Env Complaint); Fire 3.5% / **14.6%** ($2,085,312) / 3.82d / 59.6% (Plan Review).
- 311 file (500 requests FY2024, 437 closed / 63 open, weighted avg **10.8 days**, 10.1% over 30 days, satisfaction 3.63): codes DPR=Parks, DSNY=Sanitation, DOT=Transportation, **DHS=Health Services** (categories are food safety/restaurant/rodent/water — documented mapping assumption), FDNY=Fire. Satisfaction lowest for DOT (3.36).
- **All 8 below-65%-on-time processes are Manual** (Manual avg 63.6% on-time / 5.9% err / 16.1d vs Automated 94.8% / 1.4% / 1.1d) — key cross-cutting bottleneck neither proposal addresses directly.

Gross OT savings $691,991 (Sanitation $97,032 + Parks $45,396 + Fire fills $360,000 [7,500 hrs] + Fire scheduling $189,563) less Fire fill payroll $328,665 (in-budget reallocation) → **net annual $531,991; Yr1 net +$41,996**; 27 FTE reallocated; capacity converted $1,395,941; vacancy 9.1%→**4.9%** (T 6.0%, H 8.3%, F 0%); Fire cap: excess 13,618 hrs/$653,664, residual 2,169 hrs/$104,112 to FY2026; avg311 10.8→9.5.
- **Comparison**: savings A $517,954 vs B $531,991; Yr1 A $108,977 vs B $41,996; FTE A 4 vs B 27; SLA lift A +2.9 vs B +6.9 (red 6 vs 3); complexity A 3 vs B 4; risk A 3 vs B 2; **net scores (savings 25%/SLA 30%/complexity 20%/risk 25%; savings norm $300–700K, SLA norm +3–9 pts): A 1.81 vs B 2.89**.
- **Recommendation (final, use everywhere):** Adopt **Proposal B as primary framework + A-lite**: (1) B's centralized hiring + cross-training pools + shared OT budget; (2) voluntary Sanitation–Transportation **Shared Fleet & Routing Compact** (no formal merger) to capture A's ~$129K OT-sharing benefit; (3) **automation triage** on the 8 manual red processes; 12-month review gate.

MEMO

TO: Members of the City Council, City of Greenfield
FROM: Office of Management and Budget — Management Analysis Unit
DATE: October 19, 2026
RE: Departmental Restructuring Decision — Analysis of Proposal A (Consolidation) and Proposal B (Targeted Fix), with Recommended Hybrid Approach

1. Purpose and Recommendation Summary

This memorandum presents the cost-benefit analysis supporting the Council's upcoming vote on the departmental restructuring. Two proposals were modeled against the FY2024 baseline:

- Proposal A ("Consolidate") merges Health Services and Parks & Recreation into a Community Wellness department, and Sanitation and Transportation into a Public Works department; Fire remains standalone.
- Proposal B ("Targeted Fix") retains all five departments and adds a centralized hiring unit for high-vacancy divisions, cross-training pools, and shared overtime budgets for departments exceeding a 10% overtime-to-regular-hours threshold.

Recommended action: Adopt Proposal B as the primary operating framework, supplemented by (i) a voluntary Sanitation–Transportation "Shared Fleet & Routing Compact" that captures the interdepartmental coordination benefit Proposal A sought through full merger, without the governance risk, and (ii) an automation triage program targeting the eight manual, below-threshold processes. Head-to-head, Proposal B produces marginally higher annual savings ($531,991 vs $517,954), nearly seven times the service-delivery improvement (SLA lift +6.9 vs +2.9 points; below-threshold processes reduced from 8 to 3 vs 8 to 6), a lower implementation risk rating (2 vs 3 on a 5-point scale), and a materially larger workforce stabilization effect (27 FTE reallocated vs 4). A weighted net score (savings 25%, SLA improvement 30%, complexity 20%, risk 25%) yields 2.89 for B versus 1.81 for A.

2. Situation Overview: Staffing Health and Service Outcomes

2.1 Workforce position. Greenfield's five operating departments are authorized for 596 positions; 542 are filled, leaving 54 vacancies (9.1%). Payroll is $28.39M; overtime adds $4.35M (9.6% of 1,141,177 regular hours), for total personnel cost of $32.74M.

Table 1 — FY2024 department scorecard (red flags: vacancy >12%, OT >10%, on-time <65%)

[table]

Three findings stand out:

1. Vacancy is concentrated, not evenly distributed. All eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger are in Transportation (14.8–15.8% by division) and Health Services (13.6–18.2%); together these divisions hold 230 authorized positions and 36 vacancies (15.7%). Transportation's 14.9% departmental vacancy rate and Health's 16.7% are the direct drivers of the citywide 9.1%.
2. Overtime is a Fire Department problem first. Fire accounts for 47.9% of citywide OT spend ($2.09M of $4.35M) at the highest rate in the workforce ($48.00/hr) and exceeded the 10% OT-to-regular-hours threshold in all 12 months of FY2024. Sanitation sits on the watchlist (9.8% annual, but above 10% in four winter months — 52.9% of its annual OT falls in November–March, $342,302), while Parks is summer-concentrated (44.6% of its OT in May–August, $202,540). The two seasonal patterns are complementary — an argument for cross-training rather than merger.
3. Service outcomes track staffing health. Transportation has the worst 311 performance (13.6-day average resolution; 45.2-day Street Resurfacing cycle against a 30-day target; 48.3% on-time) and the lowest satisfaction (3.36/5.0). Health Services' high-priority requests average 13.9 days — the worst in the city. Citywide, of 500 FY2024 311 requests, 437 closed and 63 remain open; the weighted average resolution is 10.8 days; 44 requests (10.1%) exceeded 30 days; weighted satisfaction is 3.63/5.0.

2.4 The cross-cutting bottleneck is automation, not structure. Of 25 mapped processes, the 8 below the 65% on-time threshold are all Manual. Manual processes average 63.6% on-time, 5.9% error, and 16.1-day cycles; Semi-Automated average 80.8% / 3.7% / 4.1 days; Automated 94.8% / 1.4% / 1.1 days. Neither proposal as written addresses this gap (see Recommendation, §7).

3. NYC Benchmark Context

3.1 Staffing trends (NYS Comptroller, Report 2-2025). New York City's post-pandemic experience frames Greenfield's choices. Citywide vacancy peaked at 8.4% (Dec 2022) and stood at 5.1% in January 2024 — still 2.5x the pre-pandemic 2.0%. Greenfield's 9.1% exceeds every NYC analog: DOT 10.0% (historical 8.6%), DOHMH 9.3% (11.3%), DPR 1.7% (4.5%), DSNY ~0%, FDNY 1.4%. Attrition rose from 19,080 (pre-pandemic YTD) to 25,966 (FY2023) before easing to 21,503 (FY2024); FDNY attrition ran +52% above pre-pandemic — mirroring Greenfield's Fire OT problem. Citywide OT spend reached $1.8B through March 2024 versus $1.1B three years earlier, with OT rising from 7.0% to 10.8% of payroll; FDNY's Fire Extinguishment division OT share hit 40.3% (from 28.9%) — the same structural pattern Greenfield sees locally (Fire 14.6%, all 12 months above threshold). NYC's remedy — centralized, faster civil-service processing (DCAS exam turnaround cut from 318 to 169 days) — is the evidence base for Proposal B's centralized hiring unit.

3.2 Service-delivery benchmarks (NYC MMR). [table]

- MMR table rows:
- DOT pothole repair % meeting time-to-close standard (30 days): 100% vs 98% target
- DOHMH food establishment inspection SLA: 90% vs 90%
- DOHMH birth certificate avg response: 2.6 days vs 3.0 target
- FDNY EMS life-threatening response: 9:32 vs 6:55 target (miss)
- FDNY structural fire response: 4:37 vs 4:14 (miss)
- DPR rec center attendance 15,808/mo; DSNY paper recycling revenue $13/ton

Lessons: (i) large agencies can sustain near-perfect performance on routine, well-staffed processes (potholes) even amid citywide stress; (ii) response-time services degrade when staffing tightens (FDNY EMS misses) — relevant to Greenfield Fire's OT dependence; (iii) NYC benchmarks are useful directional context but Greenfield's budget-per-employee runs at 4–18% of NYC analogs (Table 3), so NYC-scale solutions must be scaled to Greenfield's capacity.

3.3 Per-employee budget comparison (Table 3) — NYC FY2024 modified budgets ÷ OSC headcounts vs Greenfield (payroll+OT ÷ filled): ratios 0.108 (Parks), 0.086 (Sanitation), 0.064 (Transportation), 0.041 (Health), 0.184 (Fire). Caveat: NYC figures include fringe and OTPS; used directionally to size programs, not as parity targets.

4. Proposal A — "Consolidate" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: Health + Parks → Community Wellness (212 auth / 190 filled / 22 vac, 10.4%; OT $979,350 at blended $36.78/hr); Sanitation + Transportation → Public Works (242 / 215 / 27, 11.2%; OT $1,289,856 at $32.76/hr); Fire unchanged.

(a) Process bottlenecks. A relies on shared management spans and consolidated back offices to release 4 duplicated administrative FTE ($85,000 loaded each = $340,000). It does not touch the manual-process bottleneck: the eight below-threshold processes remain below threshold; modeled average SLA lift is +2.9 points, reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 6. Street Resurfacing (48.3%) and Plan Review (59.6%) see zero modeled lift.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Modeled savings: Public Works OT −10% ($128,986) and Community Wellness OT −5% ($48,968). But the merger does not touch Fire — 47.9% of citywide OT — and blends lower-rate Parks hours ($32.50) with higher-rate Health hours ($41.50), diluting the weighted rate. The 10% PW reduction assumes routing flexibility across Sanitation and Transportation that the current collective-bargaining and licensing distinctions do not yet support (assumption A-5).

(c) Service-delivery risk. Merging two 311 intake categories and two service catalogs risks a transition dip: NYC's experience with agency mergers (e.g., DOHMH formation) shows 12–18 months of process re-stabilization. Greenfield's model carries forward current-cycle times; the 63 open 311 requests and 44 over-30-day cases would transfer to new queue ownership mid-stream. Health's high-priority response (13.9 days, worst in city) inherits Parks' lower-rate staffing pool — a quality risk for time-critical public-health work.

(d) Workforce feasibility. The four de-dup FTE must come from somewhere — attrition timing is not guaranteed; forced reductions in a 9.1%-vacancy labor market would compound the attrition problem (NYC lost 25,966 workers in FY2023 alone). Vacancy concentration is unchanged: the two merged departments would hold 49 of the city's 54 vacancies, with Public Works at 11.2% and Community Wellness at 10.4% — closer to, not below, trigger levels.

Financials: annual savings $517,954; one-time implementation $150,000; Year-1 net +$108,977 (50% realization assumed on savings).

5. Proposal B — "Targeted Fix" (evaluation on four lenses)

Design: retain five departments; (i) centralized hiring unit (2 HR FTE, $150,000/yr) covering the eight divisions above the 12% vacancy trigger (230 auth, 36 vac, 15.7%); (ii) 20 targeted hires (12 Transportation, 8 Health) plus 5 Fire position fills; (iii) 40-person cross-training pool (12 Parks, 14 Sanitation, 14 Transportation) with shared OT budget authority for departments above the 10% OT threshold.

(a) Process bottlenecks. B's SLA lift is modeled at +6.9 points on the eight red processes (e.g., Street Resurfacing +10 to 58.3%; Illegal Dumping +8 to 62.2%), reducing below-65% processes from 8 to 3 — the largest of any option — by adding field capacity where the backlogs are. Residual red processes (and the manual-process finding generally) require the automation triage in §7.

(b) Overtime cost structure. Savings are built from the actual trigger evidence: Sanitation OT −$97,032 and Parks OT −$45,396 from cross-training capacity ($142,428; the complementary seasonal cycles make the pool productive year-round); Fire: 5 fills absorb 7,500 excess OT hours ($360,000 avoided at $48.00/hr) against $328,665 of in-budget payroll reallocation, plus $189,563 of scheduling-driven reduction (29% of residual excess hours), leaving a $104,112 residual to manage into FY2026. Fire's structural excess (13,618 hours, $653,664) is directly addressed — Proposal A leaves it untouched.

(c) Service-delivery risk. Lowest of the options: no department boundaries change, 311 queue ownership is stable, and the hires land in exactly the divisions with the worst SLAs (all four Transportation divisions, all four Health divisions). Modeled citywide 311 average improves from 10.8 to 9.5 days. Risk concentrates in hiring-market feasibility — 20 competitive hires in a tight market — mitigated by the centralized unit and phased onboarding (assumption B-3).

(d) Workforce feasibility. Vacancy falls from 9.1% to 4.9% (Transportation 6.0%, Health 8.3%, Fire 0.0%) — at or below NYC analogs (DOT 10.0%, DOHMH 9.3%). 27 FTE are reallocated (20 hires + 5 fills + 2 HR). Turnover in the target divisions runs 15.2–26.1%, so sustained vacancy relief requires the retention elements (cross-training, scheduling relief) — which B funds.

Financials: gross OT savings $691,991; net annual savings $531,991 (after $160,000 annual program cost); one-time cost $224,000 ($160,000 recruiting at $8,000/hire + $64,000 training at $1,600 each); Year-1 net +$41,996; capacity converted to regular time $1,395,941.

6. Comparative Assessment

Table 4 — side-by-side: annual savings, one-time, Yr1 net, FTE reallocated, SLA lift, red processes after, 311 avg after, complexity (1-5), risk (1-5), weighted score.

Scores: normalized savings ($300K–$700K band), SLA lift (+3 to +9 band); weights: savings 25%, SLA 30%, complexity 20%, risk 25%. A = 1.81; B = 2.89.

Interpretation: A wins on Year-1 cash (simple accounting: one-time cost is lower and savings hit earlier) and on structural simplicity (3 departments vs 5). B wins on everything the Council's constituents experience: on-time performance, backlog, vacancy, overtime exposure, and risk-adjusted deliverability.

7. Recommendation

Adopt Proposal B as the primary framework, with two supplements and one guardrail:

1. B framework (centralized hiring + targeted hires/fills + cross-training + shared OT budget): net annual $531,991; Yr-1 net +$41,996; vacancy 9.1%→4.9%; SLA lift +6.9; red processes 8→3.
2. A-lite: a voluntary Sanitation–Transportation Shared Fleet & Routing Compact (joint depot/fleet utilization and route coordination during Sanitation's winter OT peak — 52.9% of its annual OT — and Transportation's year-round route coverage gaps), capturing an estimated ~$129K of the OT-sharing benefit Proposal A modeled for Public Works, without merger governance risk.
3. Automation triage: commission a 90-day process-automation assessment of the eight manual, below-65% processes (all 8 red processes are Manual; Manual avg 63.6% on-time vs Automated 94.8%). This is the only lever that raises Street Resurfacing (48.3%) and Plan Review (59.6%) materially under either proposal.
4. Guardrail: 12-month review gate. Council reconvenes on measured vacancy rate, OT share of regular hours, on-time SLA compliance, and 311 backlog before FY2027 budget adoption; unused hiring appropriation lapses if milestone SLAs are not met.

Explicit assumptions (key): [list A1-A6, B1-B6 condensed]
- A: $85,000 loaded cost per de-duplicated FTE; 10% PW / 5% CW OT reduction achievable through consolidation alone; savings realization 50% in Year 1; $150,000 one-time (systems, HR, legal); no Fire impact; service-level lifts per process model (Table: SLA lifts).
- B: $8,000 fully-loaded recruiting cost per hire; $1,600 training per cross-trained employee + $10,000 annual refresher; 2 HR FTE at $150,000/yr; Fire fills sourced by intra-department reallocation (payroll $328,665, in-budget); scheduling relief = 29% of residual Fire excess hours; seasonal cross-training productive year-round; hiring phased over 9 months.

Risks and mitigations:
- Hiring market tightness (B): phased onboarding; centralized unit mirrors NYC's DCAS turnaround gains (318→169 days); contract staffing bridge.
- Fire OT structural (both; addressed by B): if attrition worsens (NYC FDNY +52%), the $104,112 residual grows; monitor monthly; mutual-aid and scheduling levers.
- Merger transition (A, if selected instead): 12–18 month service dip; 63 open 311 cases transfer risk.
- Automation triage funding: reprioritize within existing OT savings; no new appropriation required in Year 1.

8. Data Sources and Methodology

Sources: (1) Greenfield Dept Staffing & Overtime FY2024 (staffing summary, monthly OT, 25-process metrics); (2) Greenfield 311 Service Requests FY2024 (500 requests; DHS code mapped to Health Services based on category mix — food safety, restaurant inspection, rodent, water quality; documented as an assumption); (3) NYC Expense Budget selected agencies FY2023–FY2025; (4) NYC Mayor's Management Report indicators (dataset rbed-zzin, FY2026 rows in snapshot); (5) NYS Comptroller, "2024 Update on NYC Staffing Trends" (Report 2-2025).

Method: all figures computed in a single locked model (Workbook tabs 1–4 mirror this memo); benchmarks used directionally; no projection beyond FY2025 except Fire residual; rounding to nearest dollar; percentage points as stated.
